claims.text: The nanoparticles contain five or more metals in equal or near-equal atomic ratios.
The initial nanoparticles are homogeneous, single-phase solid solutions.
High configurational entropy stabilizes the solid-solution structure up to a critical temperature.
High configurational entropy prevents significant phase separation below the critical temperature.
Configurational-entropy stabilization is manifested through uniform local lattice distortions.
Local lattice distortions arise from atomic-size and electronic mismatch among the constituent metals.
An equal atomic distribution increases configurational entropy.
Equal atomic distribution causes local lattice distortions to be distributed uniformly.
Uniformly distributed strain minimizes the driving force for elemental segregation.
Above a critical temperature, thermal energy overcomes configurational-entropy stabilization.
Below the critical temperature, the nanoparticles retain a single-phase homogeneous solid solution with minimal chemical segregation.
At or above the critical temperature, elemental clustering, phase separation, or ordering becomes detectable.
Reactive gas species, external stresses, or changes in gas composition can cause deviations from the predicted temperature-dependent behavior.
The critical temperature depends on the particular metal combination and processing history.
